Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write an incident report for a two-hour outage of a payment API caused by a expired TLS certificate. Around 200 words.

Payment API outage, September 3, 2026, 14:12 to 16:16 UTC (2 hours 4 minutes), severity SEV-1.

The payment API rejected all inbound requests after its TLS certificate expired at 14:12 UTC. Clients received handshake failures, and checkout, refund, and webhook endpoints returned errors for the full outage window.

The certificate was issued for one year and set to auto-renew 30 days before expiry. The renewal job depended on a DNS-01 challenge record that a prior infrastructure change had removed. The renewal failed silently three times over the preceding month; no alert fired because monitoring checked certificate presence, not expiry date or renewal success.

Datadog paged on-call at 14:15 UTC after error rates crossed 50%. The on-call engineer confirmed the expired certificate at 14:22, issued a manual certificate via the CA's emergency path, and deployed it to the load balancer fleet at 16:16 UTC. An estimated 41,000 payment requests failed during this period. Delayed transactions totaled $187,000, of which $12,000 were not retried by clients.

We will add a certificate-expiry alert that fires 14 days out, add a renewal-success check independent of presence checks, restore the DNS-01 challenge record, and add it to infrastructure-as-code review.

Payment API outage, September 3, 2026, 14:12 to 16:16 UTC (2 hours 4 minutes), severity SEV-1.

The payment API rejected all inbound requests after its TLS certificate expired at 14:12 UTC. Clients received handshake failures, and checkout, refund, and webhook endpoints returned errors for the full outage window.

Timeline:

14:12 UTC — TLS certificate expires; all payment API requests begin failing.
14:15 UTC — Datadog pages on-call after error rates cross 50%.
14:22 UTC — On-call engineer confirms the expired certificate as root cause.
16:16 UTC — Manual certificate deployed to the load balancer fleet; service restored.

The certificate was issued for one year and set to auto-renew 30 days before expiry. The renewal job depended on a DNS-01 challenge record that a prior infrastructure change had removed, and it failed silently three times over the preceding month.

No alert fired during that month because monitoring checked certificate presence, not expiry date or renewal success.

An estimated 41,000 payment requests failed during the outage. Delayed transactions totaled $187,000, of which $12,000 were not retried by clients.

What stops this recurring:

A certificate-expiry alert will fire 14 days before expiry, independent of the renewal job. This catches the failure even if the renewal job itself stays broken.

A renewal-success check will run after each renewal attempt and alert on failure. The current check only confirms a certificate is present, which is why three failed renewals went unnoticed.

The DNS-01 challenge record will be restored this week, and DNS records required for certificate renewal will be added to infrastructure-as-code review, so a future change cannot remove one without a reviewer seeing the dependency.
